reading.body:
Austin Agrella is named on 35 Lobbying Disclosure Act filings about AI, filed through one lobbying firm, with Anthropic and AWS among the clients disclosed.

The client list is the useful part. Ten filings name Anthropic, four name Amazon Web Services, and five name Unstructured Technologies. The rest are smaller counts: three for Quasistatics, two for Edgerunner AI, one for Comcast, and ten for a client listed as IMBUE. That spread runs from frontier model developers to data infrastructure to a cable and media company, which is what AI lobbying looks like at the application and governance layer rather than at the layer of data centers and power.

The disclosed prior government positions explain the practice area. The record lists legislative work for Rep. Will Hurd, a congressional liaison role at NTIA, a White House post, staff director work on the House Homeland cybersecurity subcommittee, and a role on House Appropriations. Those are cyber, trade, and spending assignments, which map onto the questions AI companies bring to Washington. The LDA requires filers to list covered positions held in the prior twenty years, so this is a disclosure requirement rather than an allegation.

What the data does not cover matters here. It gives counts of filings per client and one bill number, HR 6875, with no amounts, no dates of activity, no text of what was lobbied, and no outcome. It also notes that a different lobbyist shares the name, so nothing here should be read as a claim about any other person. Nothing in these figures speaks to compute, buildings, or power directly.
